summary: Japan is a tea country first — green tea is the cultural default — with a serious specialty-coffee scene layered on top. Alcohol means sake, beer, whisky, and shōchū, with chūhai as the everyday casual drink.

tea_or_coffee.headline: A tea country with a world-class coffee habit
tea_or_coffee.body: Tea (especially green tea — sencha, gyokuro, hōjicha, and powdered matcha) is woven into hospitality, ceremony, and the meal itself. Free hot tea arrives before you order at most restaurants. Coffee — in the form of single-origin pour-over and the country-wide kissaten (old-school coffee parlour) tradition — is everywhere too; Japan is one of the most discerning markets in the world for specialty beans, but it sits on top of tea, not in place of it.
tea_or_coffee.tea_culture_notes: Bottled green tea (Itō En Oi Ocha) outsells every other soft drink. Cha-no-yu (the formal tea ceremony) is a distinct discipline; you can experience an introductory version in any major city. Hōjicha (roasted) is caffeine-light and the standard dinner tea.
tea_or_coffee.coffee_culture_notes: Look for kissaten for a 1960s-style siphon-brewed cup, or third-wave roasters like Onibus, Glitch, % Arabica, and Koffee Mameya. Convenience-store coffee is genuinely good — Lawson and 7-Eleven both serve respectable espresso for ~¥150.

drinks.name: Sake
drinks.made_of: Brewed (not distilled) from polished short-grain rice, water, kōji mould, and yeast. The percentage of rice polished away (seimaibuai) drives the grade.
drinks.how_to_try: Order a flight (nomikurabe) at an izakaya — three small cups of contrasting styles. Junmai daiginjō for delicate, junmai for full-bodied. Drink chilled in summer, warmed (kanzake) in winter.
drinks.where_to_try: Kurand Sake Market (all-you-can-drink, Ikebukuro/Shinjuku), Sake no Sakai (Kiyosumi-Shirakawa), or any neighbourhood izakaya.

drinks.name: Beer
drinks.made_of: Crisp Japanese-style lagers (Asahi Super Dry, Kirin Ichiban, Sapporo, Yebisu) dominate; the craft scene is now strong with Hitachino Nest, Y. Market, and Far Yeast.
drinks.how_to_try: Start a meal with a 'toriaezu, nama!' (a draft beer to begin) — the universal first order. For craft, try Spring Valley Brewery (Daikanyama) or T.Y. Harbor (Tennoz Isle).
drinks.where_to_try: Anywhere — but a beer garden on a department-store rooftop in summer is the move.

drinks.name: Japanese whisky
drinks.made_of: Built on Scottish single-malt templates by Yamazaki (Suntory, founded 1923), Hakushu, Nikka Yoichi, and Nikka Miyagikyo. Stocks are tight — many age statements have been discontinued.
drinks.how_to_try: A 'highball' (whisky + soda + ice) is the everyday drink — try it with Suntory Kakubin. For the serious stuff, find a hotel bar with a Yamazaki 12 or Hibiki Harmony pour.
drinks.where_to_try: Bar Zoetrope (Shinjuku — 300+ Japanese whiskies), Shot Bar Zoetrope, the Park Hyatt's New York Bar.

drinks.name: Shōchū
drinks.made_of: Distilled spirit made from sweet potato (imo), barley (mugi), rice (kome), or buckwheat (soba). Earthier than sake, less aggressive than vodka. Kyushu's signature drink.
drinks.how_to_try: On the rocks (rokku), with hot water (oyu-wari) for imo shōchū in winter, or with cold water (mizu-wari).
drinks.where_to_try: Any Kyushu-style izakaya; Imo Honten chain in Tokyo specialises in it.

drinks.name: Chūhai
drinks.made_of: Shōchū (or vodka) + carbonated water + fruit. Sold canned at every convenience store; Strong Zero (Suntory) is the infamous 9% version.
drinks.how_to_try: Grab a Lemon-Sour can from 7-Eleven for ¥180 and walk along the Sumida — the standard Tokyo summer evening.
drinks.where_to_try: Every conbini fridge; lemon sour bars (lemonai) in Daikanyama and Shinjuku build the whole menu around it.

drinks.name: Matcha
drinks.made_of: Stone-ground powder from shade-grown tencha leaves, whisked with hot water using a bamboo chasen. The base of the tea ceremony.
drinks.how_to_try: Order usucha (thin) at any tea house; it's bitter, vegetal, and meant to be sipped in three. Or a matcha latte from % Arabica or Mosu Cafe (Toranomon).
drinks.where_to_try: Hama-rikyū Garden tea house, Higashiya Ginza, Nakamura Tōkichi (Kyoto day trip).

drinks.name: Sencha
drinks.made_of: Steamed (not pan-fried) green tea leaves; the everyday Japanese green tea that arrives free with most meals.
drinks.how_to_try: Brewed at 70–80°C — boiling water makes it bitter. Specialty cafés will pour you three steeps from one leaf so you can taste it evolve.

drinks.name: Hōjicha
drinks.made_of: Sencha or bancha leaves roasted in a porcelain pot until brown. Toasty, low-caffeine, the standard tea after dinner.
drinks.how_to_try: Hot at any restaurant in winter; iced as a latte at Sakurai or Higashiya in summer.
drinks.where_to_try: Most restaurants and ryokan serve it free with the meal.

drinks.name: Third-wave coffee
drinks.made_of: Single-origin beans, hand-poured (V60, Kalita Wave), often roasted in-house. Tokyo has more roasters per square mile than anywhere outside Melbourne.
drinks.how_to_try: A pour-over at Onibus Nakameguro (under the train tracks), Glitch (Jimbocho), or Koffee Mameya Kakeru (the omakase coffee bar in Kiyosumi).
drinks.where_to_try: Onibus, Glitch, Koffee Mameya, % Arabica, Fuglen Tokyo.

drinks.name: Kissaten coffee
drinks.made_of: Old-school 1960s coffee parlours: dark roasts, siphon brewing, smoking permitted, jazz on vinyl. The original Japanese coffee culture.
drinks.how_to_try: Order the 'blend' (mixed dark roast) and a thick slice of pudding (purin). No laptops; just the cup, the chair, and a record.
drinks.where_to_try: Café de l'Ambre (Ginza, since 1948), Cafe Tom (Yotsuya), Gallery Cafe Bar Kissa Sakaiki (Yanaka).
